topic: Broker Compensation, Commissions, and Referral Fees
question: Under Colorado's broker remuneration statute, a real estate broker who is registered as being in the employ of another broker may lawfully accept a commission or valuable consideration for their brokerage acts from whom?
choice_a: The broker's employer, who must be a licensed real estate broker
choice_b: Any buyer or seller in the transaction
choice_c: Another cooperating broker regardless of that broker's employment status
explanation: Section 12-10-221 makes it unlawful for a broker registered as in the employ of another broker to accept a commission from anyone except the broker's employer, and that employer must be a licensed real estate broker.

topic: Broker Compensation, Commissions, and Referral Fees
question: A broker finds a purchaser who is ready, willing, and able to complete the purchase of real estate as proposed by the owner, but the owner simply refuses to consummate the sale. Is the broker entitled to a commission?
choice_a: No, because the sale was never actually consummated
choice_b: No, unless the purchaser first forfeits earnest money to the owner
choice_c: Yes, because the sale was defeated by the owner's refusal or neglect to consummate as agreed
choice_d: Yes, but only after the broker sues the owner and obtains a judgment
explanation: Section 12-10-301 provides that a broker is entitled to a commission for finding a ready, willing, and able purchaser once the purchase is consummated or is defeated by the refusal or neglect of the owner to consummate as agreed upon.

topic: Broker Compensation, Commissions, and Referral Fees
question: A proposed purchaser refuses to complete a contract of purchase because of defects in the owner's title. Under what circumstance does the broker remain entitled to a commission despite this refusal?
choice_a: Never; a title defect always forfeits the broker's commission
choice_b: Only if the purchaser signs a written waiver of the title defect
choice_c: Only if the broker personally pays to cure the title defect
choice_d: If, within a reasonable time, the owner has the defects corrected by legal proceedings or otherwise
explanation: Section 12-10-302 states a broker is not entitled to a commission when a purchaser refuses to complete due to title defects, unless the owner corrects those defects within a reasonable time by legal proceedings or otherwise.

topic: Broker Compensation, Commissions, and Referral Fees
question: Before an owner can be required to begin legal or other proceedings to correct a title defect, what must the broker have first secured from the proposed purchaser?
choice_b: An enforceable written contract binding the purchaser to complete the purchase whenever the title defects are corrected
choice_c: A signed listing agreement with the owner
choice_d: Written proof of the purchaser's mortgage pre-approval
explanation: Section 12-10-303 provides that the owner need not begin proceedings to correct a title defect until the broker secures from the proposed purchaser an enforceable written contract binding the purchaser to complete the purchase once the defects are corrected.

topic: Broker Compensation, Commissions, and Referral Fees
question: Under section 12-10-304(1), which of the following establishes 'reasonable cause' for the payment of a referral fee?
choice_a: A contractual cooperative brokerage relationship exists
choice_b: The referring licensee has at least five years of industry experience
choice_c: The referral was requested by the client's attorney
choice_d: The referring party belongs to the local Realtor association
explanation: Section 12-10-304(1) defines reasonable cause for a referral fee as: an actual introduction of business, a contractual referral fee relationship, or a contractual cooperative brokerage relationship -- a contractual cooperative brokerage relationship is listed, the other options are not.

topic: Broker Compensation, Commissions, and Referral Fees
question: As defined in section 12-10-304(2), what constitutes 'interference with the brokerage relationship' of a licensee?
choice_a: Advertising a property that is listed by another broker
choice_b: Contacting a buyer who is represented by another broker
choice_c: Demanding a referral fee from a licensee without reasonable cause
choice_d: Refusing to offer a cooperative commission to a selling broker
explanation: Section 12-10-304(2)(b)(II) defines 'interfere with the brokerage relationship' specifically as demanding a referral fee from a licensee without reasonable cause.

topic: Broker Compensation, Commissions, and Referral Fees
question: Under section 12-10-304(2), when is a 'brokerage relationship' considered established between a broker and a buyer, seller, landlord, or tenant?
choice_a: As soon as the broker begins showing properties to a prospective buyer
choice_b: When the broker and client reach a verbal understanding to work together
choice_c: Once the broker places a yard sign on the property
choice_d: When a written brokerage agreement is entered into between the parties, or is otherwise established by law
explanation: Section 12-10-304(2)(b)(I) states a brokerage relationship is not established until a written brokerage agreement is entered into between the parties or is otherwise established by law.

topic: Broker Compensation, Commissions, and Referral Fees
question: A person prevails in a civil action against another for improperly interfering with their brokerage relationship by demanding a referral fee without reasonable cause. What may the court award the prevailing party under section 12-10-304(3)?
choice_a: Actual damages only, with no attorney fees available
choice_b: Actual damages, an additional amount of up to three times the actual damages, plus reasonable attorney fees
choice_c: A flat statutory penalty regardless of actual damages sustained
choice_d: Suspension of the violator's real estate license
explanation: Section 12-10-304(3) entitles the prevailing party to actual damages, plus an amount the court may award up to three times the actual damages, plus reasonable attorney fees.

topic: Broker Compensation, Commissions, and Referral Fees
question: In a real estate transaction involving a federally related residential mortgage, Commission Rule 6.21 says RESPA prohibits brokers from giving or receiving a Thing of Value for referral of business. Which arrangement is expressly NOT prohibited by this rule?
choice_a: A bona fide salary, commission, or other compensation for services rendered, or a return on an ownership interest in an Affiliated Business Arrangement
choice_b: A flat referral fee paid to any settlement service provider
choice_c: A cash bonus paid to a lender for referring closings
choice_d: A gift given to a title company for referring buyers
explanation: Rule 6.21.B.1 clarifies that nothing in that subsection prohibits a person or entity from receiving a bona fide salary, commission, or other compensation for services rendered, or a return on their ownership interest in an Affiliated Business Arrangement.

topic: Broker Compensation, Commissions, and Referral Fees
question: In a real estate transaction that does NOT involve a federally related residential mortgage, when may a broker accept a placement fee or commission for referring a settlement service provider?
choice_a: Only if the fee is less than $100
choice_b: Never; disclosure does not cure the prohibition in this context
choice_c: Only after first disclosing the compensation in writing to whomever the broker is referring, at the time the referral is made
choice_d: Only if the Real Estate Commission pre-approves the arrangement
explanation: Rule 6.21.B.2 states a broker will not accept a placement fee, commission, or other Thing of Value for referring a settlement service provider unless the broker first discloses such compensation in writing to whomever they are referring, at the time of making the referral.

topic: Broker Compensation, Commissions, and Referral Fees
question: Under Rule 6.21.C, a Colorado brokerage firm may pay a referral fee to a broker licensed in another jurisdiction under which condition?
choice_a: The out-of-state broker must also hold a Colorado real estate license
choice_b: The referral fee must not exceed 10 percent of the total commission
choice_c: The out-of-state broker must personally attend the Colorado closing
choice_d: The out-of-state broker actually referred a client to the Colorado firm and resides and maintains an office in the other jurisdiction
explanation: Rule 6.21.C requires, among other conditions, that the brokerage firm or broker licensed in the other jurisdiction actually referred the client and must reside and maintain an office in that other jurisdiction.

topic: Broker Compensation, Commissions, and Referral Fees
question: A seller fails to consummate a transaction as provided in the contract, through no fault of the buyer. What right does the Brokerage Firm have to the earnest money deposit made by the buyer?
choice_a: The Brokerage Firm has no right to any portion of the earnest money deposit
choice_b: The Brokerage Firm may retain the deposit as liquidated damages
choice_c: The Brokerage Firm may retain an amount equal to its expected commission
choice_d: The Brokerage Firm must split the deposit evenly with the buyer's broker
explanation: Rule 6.22.A states that if the seller fails, refuses, neglects, or is unable to consummate the transaction through no fault of the buyer, the Brokerage Firm has no right to any portion of the earnest money deposit made by the buyer.

topic: Broker Compensation, Commissions, and Referral Fees
question: In a residential transaction, absent an adjudicated claim with a judgment entered, what is a broker prohibited from doing to secure payment of a disputed commission when the broker is not a principal in the transaction?
choice_a: Sending a written demand letter to the client requesting payment
choice_b: Filing or threatening to file a lien, lis pendens, or recording the Listing Contract to secure payment of the commission
choice_c: Filing a complaint against the client with the Real Estate Commission
choice_d: Declining to release the keys to the property until paid
explanation: Rule 6.22.B prohibits a broker, absent an adjudicated claim and judgment, from filing or threatening to file a lien, lis pendens, or recording a Listing Contract to secure payment of a commission, or otherwise clouding title, when not a principal in the residential transaction.

topic: Broker Compensation, Commissions, and Referral Fees
question: A Brokerage Firm procured a tenant who leased Commercial Real Estate in accordance with the firm's written agreement with the owner, but the compensation goes unpaid. What remedy does Rule 6.22.C permit that is NOT available in a residential transaction?
choice_a: Filing a lien against the seller's other, unrelated properties
choice_b: Recording a lis pendens against the buyer's title
choice_c: Filing a lien against the Commercial Real Estate under section 38-22.5-103 for the compensation set forth in the written agreement
choice_d: Withholding the deed until the commission is paid in full
explanation: Rule 6.22.C permits a Brokerage Firm that procured a tenant for leased Commercial Real Estate, per its written agreement with the owner, to file a lien pursuant to section 38-22.5-103 against the Commercial Real Estate for the amount of compensation set forth in that agreement.
